title: agent-chokepoint decision event stream

examples.reason: tools/list refused: 1 of 4 tool definitions are not the ones this policy approved — fetch_url is sha256:1f0a2b3c4d5e6f708192a3b4c5d6e7f8091a2b3c4d5e6f708192a3b4c5d6e7f8 and this policy approves sha256:9e8d7c6b5a4938271605f4e3d2c1b0a99e8d7c6b5a4938271605f4e3d2c1b0a9

description:
WHAT THIS IS. One JSON object per line (JSONL), append-only, flushed per event, written by an agent-chokepoint enforcement point: either the MCP proxy (`method` = 'tools/call') or the Claude Code hook (`method` = 'PreToolUse'). Both doors run the same decision engine and emit the SAME key set, so one consumer reads both. Two event shapes share the stream: a DECISION event (one per judged tool call, and one per judged tools/list) and a FORWARDING event (the proxy passing a tools/list through UNJUDGED, which is not a decision).

THE tools/list DOOR IS OPT-IN AND THE EVENT SHAPE IS HOW YOU TELL. New in 1.5.0. A proxy whose policy carries a `tool_listing:` section judges every tools/list against the tool definitions the operator approved and emits a DECISION event with method 'tools/list' (rule_id under the reserved 'listing:' prefix). A proxy whose policy does not carry that section forwards the listing and emits the FORWARDING event, exactly as every build before 1.5.0 did. A proxy process holds one policy for its lifetime, so within one `run_id` you see one shape or the other and never both, and which one tells you whether that door was armed for that run - there is no field that says so directly. Do NOT generalise that to a whole deployment: an operator fronting two upstreams runs two proxy processes and may arm one and not the other, so a stream can carry both shapes under different run ids. A run whose tools/list events are all forwarding events is a run that was not checking tool definitions at all.

WHAT IT IS NOT, AND YOU CANNOT WORK AROUND IT. Every event here is written at DECISION time, BEFORE the tool runs. There is no result event, no completion event, no bytes-transferred, no upstream error, anywhere in this stream. So a detection built on it can prove a call was ALLOWED but never that it SUCCEEDED, and can prove data was permitted to leave but never that it left. Say 'attempt' in your alert text, not 'exfiltration'. There is also no per-event id and no sequence number: if your collector can deliver a line twice, nothing in the event lets you dedupe it, so make delivery exactly-once at the transport or accept inflated counts.

COMPLETENESS. Every judged tool call emits exactly one event, and so does every judged tools/list. There is no sampling and no rate limiting on emission. But an enforcement point only sees what passes through it: a tool an agent reaches without traversing this gateway produces no line at all, and absence of an event is not evidence of absence of a call.

CLOCKS. `ts` is stamped by the enforcement point that wrote the event, from its own clock. Two doors can be two processes on two hosts, so do not assume events from different `method` values are mutually ordered to better than your clock skew. Within one `run_id` (the proxy) the order is reliable.

FLATTENING THIS INTO A TABLE. The reference mapping is `telemetry/dashboard/schema.sql` in this repo: one column per field below, JSON null -> SQL NULL, and the object-valued `arguments` stored as its JSON TEXT (not jsonb) because that field is sometimes a plain string - see its description. Every SQL example in this repo, and every Sigma rule in `telemetry/sigma/`, assumes exactly that mapping. `telemetry/samples/*.jsonl` are real events produced by real runs; test your detection against them before you deploy it. One caveat if your detection is time-windowed: the cap scenarios there compress time (a run that would take 900 seconds in production is reproduced with a 3-second cap and spans ~2.4 seconds), so a window that separates the run's early allows from its later refusals in production will contain both in the sample. Widen the window or rebase the timestamps before concluding a rule does not fire; `telemetry/README.md` has the measurement.

BOTH DOORS AT ONCE. If you deploy the hook AND route the same agent through the proxy, ONE logical tool call produces TWO events - a 'PreToolUse' from the hook and a 'tools/call' from the proxy - with the tool spelled differently at each (see `tool`). There is no correlation id tying them together. Either scope your detection to one `method`, or expect a factor-of-two on any count that spans both.

VERSIONING. This document is versioned (see `version` above); the events are not stamped with it. The KEY SET is the version signal - a change to which keys exist is a new version of this schema. Field VALUES are open-ended in one specific way: `rule_id` values are partly policy-author-defined, and new engine-reserved ids can appear inside the reserved PREFIXES without the key set changing. The set of reserved prefixes itself is closed at the seven listed under `rule_id` and is enforced by the policy loader, which refuses to load a policy whose rule claims one; adding an eighth would be a change to this document. (`taint:` is the sixth, added in 1.4.0; `listing:` is the seventh, added in 1.5.0.) The set of literal REDACTION MARKERS `arguments` and `tool` can be replaced by is closed the same way and is enumerated in their descriptions; 1.6.0 added the second `arguments` marker and 1.7.0 the second `tool` marker, bringing the closed set to four, and adding a fifth would be a change to this document. (1.8.0 added no marker and changed no key: it corrected the TRUNCATION paragraph under `arguments`, which had gone on saying the proxy does not truncate after the proxy gained a decision-line bound.)

WHO WRITES THE FILE. One writer process per file. The proxy writes the file named by its `--log-file`, one such file per proxy process; the hook writes the file named by `--log-file`/`$CHOKEPOINT_LOG`, appending one line per invocation. Concurrent writers sharing one file are not supported and line atomicity is not promised - give each enforcement point its own file and merge downstream. Note what this means for outages: a proxy whose policy FAILS TO LOAD writes exactly ONE final event - rule_id 'proxy:policy-error', verdict 'block', null tool and arguments (see rule_id) - to its --log-file or stderr, then exits without serving. Any OTHER startup failure (an unparseable flag - where --log-file itself may be the broken flag - or an upstream that cannot spawn) still exits before writing anything and produces NO event at all. The hook's equivalent failures DO produce an event ('hook:policy-error'). A silent stream is therefore still ambiguous - idle agent, a proxy dead before its flags parsed, or one that never ran - and distinguishing them needs a liveness signal from outside this stream.

WHAT THIS SCHEMA CANNOT TELL YOU - ASK THE OPERATOR OF THE DEPLOYMENT. These are properties of a particular installation, not of the event format, and no version of this document can answer them. Ask for: the deployed policy file (which rules exist, which carry which `owasp` mapping, whether it is allowlist- or denylist-shaped); the configured `limits:` values and, for a long-lived gateway, its session-recycle cadence; which doors are deployed (hook, proxy, or both in one path) and the `--agent-id` / `--server-name` values given to each; which tools in that deployment actually send data OUT of the host, since no field here distinguishes an egress tool from a local one; the deployed `taint:` settings, if any - which tools are named untrusted sources, which are named egress tools, and which of the three `egress_mode` levels is set, since that decides which 'taint:' ids can appear at all and none of it is on the event; whether the deployed policy carries a `hidden_context:` section and WHICH files it declares, since that alone decides whether the declared-hidden-context marker can appear and what its absence is worth; whether the deployed policy carries a `tool_listing:` section at all, and if so WHEN its approved digests were taken and from which build of the upstream, since a pin taken from an already-hostile server approves that server forever and nothing on the event can say so; whether the collector's delivery is exactly-once; and the retention window of whatever store you query. Threshold numbers in any detection you write from this schema alone are guesses until they are baselined against that deployment's real traffic.

ts.description: Event time, ISO 8601 with a UTC offset, e.g. '2026-08-04T16:09:32.984474+00:00'. Always UTC in every build that ships today, so lexical ordering is chronological - but it is written from the emitting process's clock (see CLOCKS in the top-level description).

agent_id.description: The agent identity the enforcement point was configured with (`--agent-id`); defaults are 'default' at the proxy and 'claude-code-hook' at the hook. NOT AUTHENTICATED and not unique: it is deployment configuration, an operator may run many agents under one value, and two deployments may share the default. It is a grouping hint, never an identity claim, and it is the wrong key to build a per-session detection on - use `run_id` where it is available.

run_id.description:
The RUN this event belongs to: a 32-character hex id, generated per proxy process. A 'run' is one MCP client session with the proxy, and it is the exact scope the `limit:*` caps are counted over - so this is the key you group by to reason about any limit, to reconstruct one agent session, or to tell one busy session apart from many quiet ones.

NULL AT THE HOOK, ALWAYS, AND THAT IS THE ANSWER RATHER THAN A GAP. The hook is one short-lived process per tool call: it holds no session, keeps no run state, and enforces no limits (which is why `limit:*` never appears with method 'PreToolUse'). Minting an id there would be worse than null - every call would look like its own run. For hook-side stateful detections, group by `agent_id` over a time window and say in the runbook that the grouping is approximate.

Also null on exactly one proxy event, 'proxy:policy-error': that startup refusal precedes the session, so the run it would identify was never created.

A long-lived deployed gateway RECYCLES its session on a cadence to keep each run inside the caps, so a healthy production stream shows `run_id` changing periodically with no gap in service. A run id that never changes while `limit:max_wall_clock_seconds` blocks start appearing is a gateway that has gone dark - see the `limit:` notes on `rule_id`.

server.description:
The MCP server identity the call was JUDGED under - the same value a policy rule's `server:` key binds to. At the proxy it is the `--server-name` the process was started with (one value for the whole process). At the hook it is the '<server>' half of a 'mcp__<server>__<tool>' name.

null means NO IDENTITY WAS CLAIMED, and it happens for three different reasons: a proxy started without `--server-name`; a native (non-MCP) Claude Code tool, which comes from no server; or a hook refusal made before the name was parsed. Treat null as 'unattributed', never as a server called 'null', and never merge it with a real server in a per-server breakdown.

OPERATOR TRAP WORTH CHECKING BEFORE YOU TRUST A PER-SERVER NUMBER: the two doors learn this string by different routes - a flag at the proxy, the tool-name prefix at the hook - and nothing makes them agree. If an operator starts the proxy with `--server-name docs` while Claude Code calls the same upstream 'mcp__docs_mcp__...', one upstream appears as two identities. Confirm the configured values before reporting per-server counts.

method.description: Which door judged what. 'tools/call' = the MCP proxy judging one tool call (the JSON-RPC method it intercepted). 'PreToolUse' = the Claude Code hook judging one tool call (the hook event it handled). 'tools/list' = the MCP proxy judging a whole tool LISTING against the definitions the operator approved (new in 1.5.0; a 'tools/list' event carrying `action` instead of `verdict` is the forwarding shape and is not a decision). This is also the field that tells you which `verdict` semantics apply - see `verdict` - and the field to branch on before reading `tool`, which is always null on a 'tools/list' decision.

tool.description:
The tool name AS IT ARRIVED at that door. The proxy logs the wire's MCP tool name ('read_file'). The hook logs Claude Code's name ('Read', 'mcp__docs-mcp__read_file'), NOT the engine name it was translated to - so the same underlying operation is spelled differently at the two doors ('Read' at the hook, 'read_file' at the proxy), and several Claude Code built-ins translate onto one engine tool. Match on `rule_id` when you want 'what judged it'; match on `tool` when you want 'what the agent asked for'.

null on a hook refusal whose input carried no readable name, on 'proxy:policy-error' - a startup refusal that precedes any call - and on EVERY method 'tools/list' decision, allow and block alike: that decision is about the listing as a whole, and the tools it names are in `reason`, in the order the upstream advertised them. Do not read a null here as 'unknown tool'; branch on `method` first.

If the NAME itself contained a detected credential, this field is replaced whole by the literal string '[REDACTED: sensitive content detected in tool name]' - an agent-supplied tool name is attacker-influenceable and is scanned like any argument.

NEW IN 1.7.0: a SECOND marker can appear here for the same reason the `arguments` field has two. If the deployed policy carries a `hidden_context:` section and the name contains a segment of the material it declares, this field is replaced whole by '[REDACTED: declared hidden context detected in tool name]'. The credential check runs FIRST, so a name carrying both carries the credential marker only. Before 1.7.0 the name path ran the credential check and nothing else, so declared material arriving in a tool NAME - one field over from the arguments where it WAS checked - was written into this field in full (B-116). The same limit applies as to the `arguments` marker: matching is literal over the declared text, so a name the operator's material does not literally contain produces no marker, and its absence does not mean the name carried none.

arguments.description:
The arguments the ENGINE judged - usually a JSON object, sometimes a plain string (see redaction), null when the wire carried none or the input was unjudgeable, and always null on a method 'tools/list' decision, which judges definitions rather than arguments. Four transformations have already happened, and each one changes what a detection can match:

1. PATH CANONICALIZATION (both doors, and ONLY the argument named 'path'). Its value is logged AFTER resolution: symlinks followed to their final target, '.' and '..' collapsed, and the spelling corrected to the case the filesystem actually holds. This is deliberate - the verdict is about the file that would really be opened, so the event pairs that verdict with that same file. THE CONSEQUENCE FOR DETECTION AUTHORS IS THE IMPORTANT PART: the classic traversal signatures ('../', an encoded '%2e%2e', a symlink's own name, a case-variant spelling) are GONE by the time they reach this field, so a rule matching them here will NEVER FIRE no matter how much traversal an agent attempts. Detect traversal by the rule that caught it (`rule_id`), or by the resolved path landing somewhere it should not - never by the literal '../'. Note the paths that are NOT resolved but REFUSED, arriving as rule_id 'pep:unresolvable-path' with the offending spelling described in `reason`: a relative path, a '~'-prefixed path (the enforcement point will not guess whose home directory the tool meant), and any path whose resolution actually failed (symlink loop, permission error). Other argument names - 'command', 'url' - are logged as the agent wrote them.

2. CREDENTIAL REDACTION (both doors). If a credential is detected ANYWHERE in the arguments, this whole field - object and all - is replaced by the literal string '[REDACTED: sensitive content detected in arguments]', whatever the verdict was, INCLUDING ON ALLOWED CALLS. The marker is therefore a reliable 'a secret was present in this call' signal that does not depend on how well the policy was authored; match it as an exact string. Detection is a fixed set of PATTERNS over known credential formats - AWS access key ids (AKIA...), GitHub token family (ghp_/gho_/ghu_/ghs_/ghr_...), Slack token family (xox...), Google API keys (AIza...), and PEM private-key headers ('-----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY-----'). It is NOT entropy-based and NOT a general secret or PII classifier: a credential in a format not on that list, and ordinary sensitive data such as customer records, source code or prose, are not detected and produce no marker. So a redacted event means a credential was present; a non-redacted event does NOT mean the call was clean.

3. DECLARED HIDDEN-CONTEXT REDACTION (both doors). NEW IN 1.6.0. If the deployed policy carries a `hidden_context:` section and any string in the arguments contains a segment of the material it declares, this whole field is replaced by a DIFFERENT literal string - '[REDACTED: declared hidden context detected in arguments]' - whatever the verdict was, INCLUDING ON ALLOWED CALLS and whether or not any rule arms the matching predicate. Two markers now exist and they state different facts: the one above means a published CREDENTIAL FORMAT was present, this one means material THIS DEPLOYMENT'S OPERATOR DECLARED was present - a system prompt, a tool-schema listing, an internal runbook. Match either as an exact string; a substring match on '[REDACTED:' finds both and is the right test for 'this field was withheld'. The credential check runs FIRST, so a call carrying both carries the credential marker only. THE LIMIT OF THIS SIGNAL, and it is the same shape as the one above: matching is LITERAL over the declared text (whitespace collapsed, ASCII case folded, segments under 32 characters dropped), so a recitation the operator's material does not literally contain - a paraphrase, or a chunk split mid-sentence across two calls - produces no marker. A marker means declared material was present; its absence does NOT mean the call carried none. Whether this can appear at all depends on that deployment's `hidden_context:` section, which is not on the event - ask the operator (see the description at the top of this schema).

4. TRUNCATION (BOTH doors, on DIFFERENT triggers). NEW IN 1.8.0, AND IT IS A CORRECTION: until this version this paragraph said the proxy does not truncate, which stopped being true when the proxy gained a bound on the line it writes. A detection built on the old sentence - one that assumes a proxy event carries whole argument values - should be re-read. At the HOOK, truncation is UNCONDITIONAL and per string: any remaining string longer than 256 characters becomes '<str len=N truncated>' - Claude Code payloads carry whole file bodies. At the PROXY, it is CONDITIONAL on the size of the finished line: an event whose JSON line is 16384 bytes or under is written exactly as it was built, so an ORDINARY proxy event is not truncated at all and you cannot assume the 256-character cut is present. Over that ceiling the proxy runs the hook's own per-string walk - the same 256-character cut, the same '<str len=N truncated>' spelling - and if the line is STILL over, every remaining field longer than 256 characters is replaced by '<N bytes omitted: over the 16384-byte decision-line bound>'. That last string is proxy-only and it says the LINE hit its ceiling: it is NOT a redaction marker and does not mean anything was detected. One proxy event is deliberately outside the bound - the 'proxy:policy-error' startup refusal, whose fields are the operator's own rather than anything an agent supplied. ORDER IS GUARANTEED AND IT MATTERS, AT BOTH DOORS: BOTH redaction checks run on the FULL untruncated arguments before any truncation, so a secret - or a declared segment - padded past either boundary is still detected and still redacts the whole field. A redaction marker is short, so it survives both proxy stages unchanged and an exact-string match on it still works on a bounded line.

At the hook a translated native call carries the ORIGINAL payload plus the canonical key the translation added, so a 'Read' shows both 'file_path' and 'path' with the same value.

EXACT ENCODING, because a detection matching the redaction marker depends on it: `arguments` is an ordinary JSON VALUE on the line - a JSON object normally, a JSON STRING when redacted - so `json.loads(line)['arguments']` yields a Python dict or the bare marker string with no surrounding quotes. See this schema's `examples`. If your collector stores the field as JSON TEXT (which is what telemetry/dashboard/schema.sql does, and why that column is `text` rather than `jsonb`), the object case becomes '{"path": ...}' and the redacted case becomes the bare marker without added quotes. Key ORDER in that text follows the order the agent sent, and is NOT normalised - so string equality on this field is not a reliable 'same call' test even for genuinely identical calls. Use the engine's own repeat counter instead (see `rule_id`, limit:max_repeated_identical_calls), which compares a key-sorted signature.

verdict.description:
The engine's answer. 'block' is a refusal at both doors: the call never reached the tool.

'ask' MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS AT THE TWO DOORS AND YOU MUST BRANCH ON `method`:
  - method 'tools/call' (proxy): 'ask' FAILS CLOSED. No approval channel is wired, so the call was REFUSED with JSON-RPC error -32001. Count it with the refusals.
  - method 'PreToolUse' (hook): 'ask' was handed to Claude Code's interactive permission prompt, and a human MAY HAVE APPROVED IT. The call may well have executed. This stream does NOT record how the prompt was answered. Do not count these as refusals and do not count them as executions - they are an indeterminate class, and closing an alert on one needs evidence from outside this stream.

'allow' means the engine permitted the call: at the proxy the arguments were then forwarded to the upstream server; at the hook the tool was permitted to run in-process. Neither is a statement that it succeeded.

Other JSON-RPC codes the proxy uses for its own refusals, all of which appear here as verdict 'block': -32000 blocked by a rule, -32002 uninspectable input channel, -32003 unresolvable path. The hook's three Claude Code outcomes (allow / ask / deny) map onto this field as 'allow' / 'ask' / 'block' - the string written here is 'block', never 'deny'.

rule_id.description:
What produced the verdict. MATCH BY PREFIX, NOT BY AN EXHAUSTIVE LIST - new ids can appear inside a reserved namespace without this schema's key set changing.

Seven prefixes are RESERVED for decisions no policy rule produced, and the policy loader REFUSES to load a policy whose rule claims one - so a bare id and a namespaced id can never be confused:
  - 'default:on_no_match' - no rule matched; the policy's deny-by-default answered. This is the ordinary background noise of a deny-by-default policy, not an attack signal, and it carries no `owasp` value.
  - 'limit:max_tool_calls_per_run' | 'limit:max_wall_clock_seconds' | 'limit:max_repeated_identical_calls' - a per-run cap tripped. Counted over one `run_id`, PROXY ONLY (the hook enforces no limits). Caps are evaluated BEFORE any policy rule and the first exceeded cap answers immediately, so once a call-count or wall-clock cap trips, EVERY later call in that run carries that same limit id - no policy rule and no 'default:on_no_match' can appear after it. A run whose events go from 'allow' to an unbroken tail of one 'limit:' id is a session that has stopped being served. Emission is unaffected: every judged call still produces exactly one event, so the tail is visible rather than silent. max_wall_clock_seconds is measured from the start of the run regardless of activity, so an idle long-lived run can trip it with no user in sight. max_repeated_identical_calls is scoped to one repeated call SIGNATURE rather than to the whole run, which is what makes it the blocked-then-retry-loop signal; the signature is a key-sorted serialisation of the tool name plus the arguments AS THE AGENT SENT THEM (before canonicalization, redaction or truncation), and it counts every attempt including the refused ones - which is precisely why a loop of blocked retries trips it.
  - 'proxy:uninspectable-input-channel' - the call carried multi-round-trip input the engine cannot inspect; refused rather than passed.
  - 'proxy:policy-error' - the proxy's policy failed to load at startup; exactly one such event is written and the proxy exits without serving ('hook:policy-error', at the other door). The ONE decision event that corresponds to no tool call: tool and arguments are null, run_id is null (the run it would identify was never created), owasp is null, decision_ms is 0.0.
  - 'proxy:uninspectable-listing' - NEW IN 1.5.0. A tools/list response the proxy could not reduce to approvable tool definitions (no `tools` array, a tool with no usable name, two definitions under one name, or a definition that will not serialise); refused rather than passed through unjudged. Only possible where a `tool_listing:` section is deployed, since an unarmed proxy never parses a listing at all.
  - 'pep:unresolvable-path' - a path could not be canonicalized; refused rather than judged unresolved.
  - 'hook:unparseable-input' | 'hook:policy-error' - the hook could not parse its input or load its policy, and failed closed.
  - 'taint:secret-egress' | 'taint:new-domain-egress' | 'taint:egress' - NEW IN 1.4.0. The run had already consumed a result from a tool the policy names an untrusted source, and then made a call to a tool the policy names an egress tool. PROXY ONLY, for the same reason the limit ids are (the hook holds no run). All three carry owasp 'LLM01'. The id says WHAT THE GATEWAY SAW, not which strictness level the operator configured - 'taint:secret-egress' means the outbound arguments carried a known credential format, 'taint:new-domain-egress' means the call named a host outside the deployment's post-taint allowlist, 'taint:egress' means the operator refuses ALL outbound calls after taint. Which of the three can appear at all depends on that deployment's `taint.egress_mode`, which is not on the event - ask the operator (see the description at the top of this schema).

READ THESE EVENTS PRECISELY. A taint id means an outbound call was REFUSED after the run consumed untrusted content. It does NOT mean an injection was detected: nothing here inspects the consumed content, and taint is set on the SOURCE tool, not on anything in the result. A run can be tainted by an entirely benign page. Say 'refused an outbound call from a run that had read untrusted content' in your alert text, not 'blocked a prompt injection'. Conversely, a run with no taint events is not a clean run - it may simply never have called a source tool.

  - 'listing:approved' | 'listing:unpinned-tool' | 'listing:definition-drift' | 'listing:definition-changed-mid-run' - NEW IN 1.5.0, method 'tools/list' only, PROXY ONLY (the hook never sees a listing). All four carry owasp 'LLM04'. 'listing:approved' is an ALLOW and is the only allow verdict any reserved prefix emits: every advertised definition matched a digest the operator approved. The other three are refusals of the WHOLE listing, and the id says which fact the gateway saw: 'listing:unpinned-tool' - the listing carried a tool this policy approves no definition of; 'listing:definition-drift' - a tool it DOES approve arrived with a different definition; 'listing:definition-changed-mid-run' - this run had already been handed a different definition of that same tool, which no benign server upgrade can produce inside one `run_id`. When a listing breaks more than one of these, the most specific true one supplies the id and `reason` names every offender with the digest computed for it.

READ THESE EVENTS PRECISELY TOO. A 'listing:' refusal is an INTEGRITY finding, not a content one. Nothing here reads a description, scores one, or forms any opinion about what one says: a harmless typo fix in a description produces the same verdict and the same rule id as a description carrying hidden instructions, because the only question asked is whether the definition is the one the operator approved. Say 'served a tool definition the operator has not approved' in your alert text, not 'blocked a poisoned tool'. And the converse costs more than it looks: 'listing:approved' means the definitions match the approved digests, NOT that they are safe - a pin taken from a server that was already hostile approves that server indefinitely, and no field here can tell you when the pin was taken. It is also a statement about the DEFINITIONS and not about the response that carried them: a tools/list result has fields of its own, and two of them - '_meta' and 'nextCursor' - are upstream-controlled free text that belongs to no tool definition, is covered by no digest, and reaches the client verbatim on an approved listing (measured, with a paired refusal for the same text inside a definition: docs/LIMITATIONS.md section 20 item 6, and D-040 for why nothing here judges it). Say 'the tool definitions matched the approved digests' in your alert text, not 'the listing was clean'.

Any OTHER value is a rule id from the policy file, chosen by the policy author (e.g. 'fs-read-scoped', 'shell-destructive'). They are stable within a deployment but not portable between deployments: a detection that hard-codes one is deployment-specific, which is why the rules in `telemetry/sigma/` key on `owasp` and on the reserved prefixes instead.

owasp.description:
The OWASP LLM Top-10 mapping of the rule that fired. The policy loader ENFORCES the format 'LLM' followed by exactly two digits ('LLM01', 'LLM02', 'LLM10'), so you will never see 'LLM01:2025', a full title, or lower case - a policy spelling it any other way does not load. Every `limit:*` decision carries 'LLM10', every `taint:*` decision carries 'LLM01', and every `listing:*` decision carries 'LLM04' - the ONE leg of Supply Chain that reaches this gateway, since that document's own scenarios are model-artifact ones and it routes MCP servers and tool registries to OWASP's separate Agentic Supply Chain document.

WHICH mapping a rule carries is the policy author's choice, not something the engine derives, so treat it as a well-formed but author-supplied label: LLM01 for the injection-class enforcement this gateway exists for, LLM02 for sensitive-data egress. Before relying on it, check how disciplined the deployed policy's tagging is.

null whenever no policy rule supplied one: 'default:on_no_match' and every 'hook:' refusal. That null is useful - it is what separates a rule the author WROTE from the deny-by-default noise floor.

reason.description: Human-readable sentence for the decision, engine- or enforcement-point-authored. Fine for an analyst to read; a poor thing to match on - it may quote the tool name, and a tool name is agent-supplied text. If the name was redacted, the same marker is substituted here too, so a credential never survives one field over.

decision_ms.description: Engine decision latency in milliseconds, 3 decimal places - the time spent in the pure decision function, not the tool's own runtime. Exactly 0.0 marks a refusal made BEFORE the engine ran (uninspectable channel, unresolvable path, every 'hook:' refusal, 'proxy:policy-error'), so exclude 0.0 from latency statistics or you will report a latency the engine never spent.

forwardingEvent.description: The proxy forwarding a tools/list request upstream UNJUDGED. Carries no verdict - it is discovery traffic that crossed the gateway without being checked, which is what a deployment whose policy has no `tool_listing:` section does with every listing. The hook has no equivalent. Filter these out of decision analytics by `verdict` being present, NOT by method: since 1.5.0 an armed deployment emits method 'tools/list' DECISION events, so `method IN ('tools/call','PreToolUse')` now drops real verdicts.
